items.stem: If P(A) = 0.3, then P(not A) = 0.7.

opts.why: Complement rule: 1 − 0.3.
The mix-up: none here; A and not A always add to 1.

items.stem: P(A ∪ B) can be larger than P(A) + P(B).

opts.why: The mix-up: forgetting which way the overlap correction goes.
Corrected: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B), which is at most P(A) + P(B).

items.stem: The letters of BOOK can be arranged in 4! = 24 distinct ways.

opts.why: The mix-up: treating the two O’s as different letters.
Corrected: 4! / 2! = 12, because swapping the two O’s gives the same word.

items.stem: Three fair coins are flipped. What is P(exactly two heads)?

opts.why: HHT, HTH, THH: 3 of the 8 equally likely sequences.
That is P(at least two heads) = 4/8.
Treats “0, 1, 2, 3 heads” as four equally likely outcomes; they are not.
Two heads out of three coins is a ratio of counts, not a probability.

items.why: List the 8 sequences and count those with exactly two H.

items.stem: How many 5-card hands from a standard 52-card deck contain all four aces?

opts.why: The four aces are fixed; the fifth card is any of the 48 non-aces.
Orders the aces, but a hand is unordered.
Counts the aces themselves, not hands.
Counts the hands that do not contain all four aces.

items.why: Fix what must be there, then count the free choices.

items.stem: In a dorm, 60% of students take French, 50% take Spanish, and 90% take at least one of the two. What fraction take both?

opts.why: 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.9: inclusion–exclusion solved for the overlap.
0.6 · 0.5 assumes the two choices are independent, which nothing here says.
0.9 − 0.5 is the fraction taking French but not Spanish.
0.6 + 0.5 counts the overlap twice and is not even a probability.

items.why: “At least one” is the union, so rearrange P(F ∪ S) = P(F) + P(S) − P(F ∩ S).

items.stem: Which lists of outcomes are equally likely?

opts.why: Yes: a fair die by definition.

opts.t: Two fair coins: {0 heads, 1 head, 2 heads}
opts.why: No: 1 head happens two ways (HT, TH), so it has probability 1/2.
No: sum 7 has six ordered pairs, sum 2 has one.

opts.t: One card from a shuffled deck: {hearts, diamonds, clubs, spades}
opts.why: Yes: 13 cards in each suit.

items.why: An outcome list is equally likely only if each item covers the same number of underlying equally likely cases.

items.stem: How many ways are there to choose 2 people out of 6 when order does not matter?
A fair die is rolled 3 times. What is P(no six at all)? Give 3 decimals or an expression.
items.why: Each roll avoids a six with probability 5/6, and the rolls are independent.

items.stem: If P(B) > 0 and P(A | B) = P(A), then A and B are independent.

opts.why: Equivalent definition: multiply both sides by P(B) to get P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B).
The mix-up: thinking independence needs a separate check beyond this equation.

items.stem: Whenever P(B) > 0, P(A | B) + P(A<sup>c</sup> | B) = 1.

opts.why: Conditioning on B gives a probability measure on B, and A, A<sup>c</sup> split it.
The mix-up: confusing it with P(A | B) + P(A | B<sup>c</sup>), which need not be 1.

items.stem: A positive result on a test that is right 99% of the time means you have the condition with probability 99%.

opts.why: The mix-up: reading P(+ | condition) as P(condition | +).
Corrected: P(condition | +) also depends on the base rate. For a rare condition it can be far below 99%.

items.stem: Two cards are drawn from a shuffled deck without replacement. What is P(both are aces)?

opts.why: First ace 4/52; given that, 3 aces remain among 51 cards.
That is with replacement; here the first ace is gone.
Adds where the multiplication rule multiplies.
Doubles a single-draw probability, which is not how “and” works.

items.why: Multiplication rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(A) P(B | A).

items.stem: 20% of emails are spam. A filter flags 95% of spam and 10% of normal email. An email is flagged. Which is closest to P(spam | flagged)?

opts.why: That is P(flagged | spam), the other direction.
That is P(spam and flagged), the numerator only.
That is P(flagged), the denominator only.

items.stem: A and B are independent with P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A ∪ B)?

opts.why: Forgets to subtract the overlap.
That is P(A ∩ B).
1 − 0.2 is the complement of the intersection, not the union.

items.why: Independence gives the overlap 0.2; then use inclusion–exclusion.

items.stem: A fair die is rolled and A = {the roll is even}. For which events B are A and B independent?

opts.why: Dependent: disjoint from A.

items.why: Compute P(A ∩ B) and compare with P(A) P(B) for each option.

items.stem: P(B) = 0.25 and P(A | B) = 0.4. What is P(A ∩ B)?
E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] holds only when X and Y are independent.

opts.why: The mix-up: carrying over the condition that E[XY] = E[X]E[Y] needs.
Corrected: linearity of expectation always holds, dependent or not.

items.stem: Adding the same constant to every value of X leaves Var(X) unchanged.

opts.why: Var(X + b) = Var(X): the whole distribution slides, the spread stays.
The mix-up: thinking a bigger mean means a bigger variance.

items.stem: If Var(X) = 0, then X equals a single value with probability 1.

opts.why: An average of non-negative squares is 0 only if each square with positive probability is 0, so X = E[X].
The mix-up: thinking zero variance means X is zero; it means X is constant.

items.stem: X ~ Binomial(8, 0.25). What is E[X]?

opts.why: That is the variance np(1 − p).
That is p, the chance of one success.
n(1 − p) is the expected number of failures.

items.why: Sum of 8 Bernoulli(0.25) indicators, each with mean 0.25.

items.stem: A game pays $12 with probability 0.25 and costs you $5 otherwise. What are your expected winnings per play?

opts.why: 12 − 5 ignores the probabilities.
0.25 · 12 counts the win and forgets the loss.
(12 − 5) / 2 weights both outcomes equally.

items.why: Weight each payoff by its probability.

items.stem: E[X] = 2 and E[X<sup>2</sup>] = 13. What is Var(X)?

opts.why: 13 − 2 forgets to square the mean.
That is the standard deviation, √9.
13 + 4 adds where the formula subtracts.

items.stem: X ~ Bernoulli(0.3). Which are correct?

opts.why: Wrong: X<sup>2</sup> = X for a 0/1 variable, so E[X<sup>2</sup>] = 0.3. 0.09 is (E[X])<sup>2</sup>.
Wrong: P(X = 1) = p = 0.3.

items.why: For 0/1 variables, X<sup>2</sup> = X is the shortcut.

items.stem: A raffle ticket wins $10 with probability 0.1, wins $2 with probability 0.3, and wins nothing otherwise. What are the expected winnings per ticket, in dollars?
items.why: Multiply each payout by its probability and add; the “nothing” outcome contributes 0.

items.stem: A city's daily temperature C (in °C) has Var(C) = 4. In Fahrenheit, F = 1.8C + 32. What is Var(F)?
items.why: Var(aX + b) = a<sup>2</sup> Var(X): square the 1.8, and the + 32 shift drops out.
